newsitem.title: USA: Swiss took stolen gold after Sweden refused -document.
newsitem.headline: Swiss took stolen gold after Sweden refused -document.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank took in 100 tonnes of gold from the Nazis in 1943 after Sweden refused because the bullion had been stolen by Germany from Belgium, according to a Second World War document released on Thursday.

The document, a 1946 report by the U.S. political affairs adviser for the American occupation government then ruling Germany, was released by Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, a New York Republican and a severe critic of Swiss actions during and after the war.

D'Amato, who is pressing for re-opening a 1946 treaty with the Swiss on the return of looted gold, said, "A truly neutral country would not have accepted this gold, knowing that the gold had in fact been looted from one of its neighbouring countries."

The Allies had warned neutral nations in January 1943 not to accept gold stolen from Nazi-occupied countries because the Germans were using it to buy supplies in neutral countries to further their war efforts.
Germany started the Second World War with between $70 million and $100 million in its gold reserves. According to documents, it ended the war with $748 million worth of the precious metal.

In the 1946 Washington accord signed with Britain, the United States and France, Switzerland agreed to return $60 million worth of the gold it handled for Germany, although the United States believed it had about $400 million.
The 1946 document said the Swiss accepted the 100 tonnes of stolen Belgian gold, worth $123 million at the time, after it had been rejected by Sweden.
"How can the Swiss claim they acted in good faith when this gold was acquired at the time ... when they knew it had been refused by the Swedes ...," the document said.
